title: From Graphs to Teams
objective: After this lesson you will be able to decide single-graph vs multi-agent by coordination needs, name the coordination costs teams pay (handoff formats, delegation logic, compounded errors, context growth), and draw team boundaries that justify themselves.
why: The LangGraph course ended at subgraphs and supervisors — this course starts where composition becomes collaboration: multiple specialized agents with distinct mandates, tools, and authority. Teams are not 'more agents' but a different coordination regime with its own economics. Choosing it for fixed pipelines buys overhead; refusing it for variable specialist work buys monoliths that can't delegate.

blocks.text: Field a team when work needs **variable delegation** (who handles this ticket? depends), **distinct authority** (pricing vs support vs fraud touch different powers), or **parallelizable specialties** (research while drafting). Keep a single graph when the pipeline is fixed, authority is uniform, and one specialty suffices. The test from LangGraph Ch.1 generalizes: delete the delegation — collapse means the team earns its keep.

Teams charge four taxes: **handoff formats** (every transfer needs contracted shapes), **delegation logic** (routers/managers with their own tests), **compounded errors** (three 95% agents ≈ 86% pipeline — multiply, don't average), and **context growth** (each agent adds its slice). Price the bill before staffing: if specialization gains don't exceed coordination taxes, the team is theater with latency.

blocks.caption: Multiplicative reliability, additive context — the team P&L

blocks.text: Boundary drawing: what becomes a team

Draw boundaries at **authority and specialty seams**: pricing decisions (money authority) separate from support drafting (communication skill) separate from fraud review (risk authority). Never split by *steps* of one specialty (research-1, research-2) — that multiplies handoffs without specialization gains. One team per bounded context; subgraphs (LangGraph Ch.8) for reuse *within* a context.

blocks.title: Price the team
blocks.note: Run it: team acc 0.913 vs solo 0.9 (marginal gain) at 4400 vs 2000 tokens (2.2x cost). Verdict says team — barely. Change one agent to 0.9 and re-run: the verdict flips, proving coordination math decides, not enthusiasm.

items: Teams for variable delegation, distinct authority, parallelizable specialties — graphs for fixed uniform pipelines
Price coordination: multiplicative reliability, additive context, handoff formats, delegation tests
Boundaries at authority/specialty seams; subgraphs for reuse within contexts

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice pricer and record the verdict. (b) Drop one team agent to 0.9 accuracy and re-run; record the flip. (c) Decide team-vs-graph for: nightly catalog audit (fixed checks) vs dispute desk (refunds/fraud/VIP mix) — with the deletion/coordinator test applied to each.
hints: Baseline: team 0.913 > solo 0.9 (verdict team). One weak link (0.9): 0.97×0.97×0.9 ≈ 0.847 < 0.9 (verdict flips to solo).
Catalog audit: fixed checks, uniform authority → single graph (delete delegation: nothing breaks). Dispute desk: variable routing across authorities → team (deletion collapses behavior).
State the coordination bill each choice pays: audit pays nothing; desk pays handoffs+tests for specialization gains.
exercise.why: Sensitivity analysis (one weak agent flips the verdict) teaches that team reliability is a weakest-link game — composition demands per-agent bars, not averages. The two decisions practice boundary drawing on opposite archetypes.
exercise.code: // Sensitivity pattern: vary one accuracy, watch the verdict flip.

quiz.q: Fixed triage→decide→draft pipeline, uniform authority. Team or graph?
options: Single graph: fixed pipeline pays zero coordination bill — teams add handoffs for no gain
quiz.explain: No variability, no authority split, no parallel specialties: coordination taxes buy nothing. Graph it.

options: ≈86% (multiplicative: 0.95³) — each handoff must earn its error share
quiz.explain: Series reliability multiplies. Team design must beat solo accuracy *after* compounding — per-agent bars, not averages.

quiz.q: Where do you split one team into two?
options: At authority/specialty seams (pricing vs support) — never by subdividing one specialty's steps
quiz.explain: Seams follow authority and skill boundaries: independent mandates, distinct powers, separate eval. Step-splitting multiplies handoffs without gains.

summary: Teams for variability, authority splits, parallel specialties — priced in multiplicative reliability and additive context. Boundaries at seams; deletion test decides.
